## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saccaṁkirajātaka* (Ja 73) is a narrative included in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon. The frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), where the Buddha addresses the assembly of monks discussing the persistent wickedness and murderous intent of Devadatta [Fausböll 1877]. The Buddha notes that this was not the first time Devadatta had attempted to kill him and relates an account of their past lives [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta rescues a drowning, wicked prince alongside a snake, a rat, and a parrot [Anandajoti 2010; Pragati Sahni 2008]. The rat and snake had previously been human beings who, dominated by greed and anxiety over their hoarded wealth, were reborn in animal form [Scott 2009]. Later, when the ungrateful prince ascends the throne, he encounters the Bodhisatta in the royal city and vindictively orders him flogged and marched out to be executed, whereas the Bodhisatta remains patient and steadfast [Anandajoti 2010]. In contrast to the ungrateful monarch, the animals remain loyal and repay their savior [Anandajoti 2010; Pragati Sahni 2008]. The Bodhisatta eventually becomes king and rewards the animals with extravagant care, fashioning a golden tube for the snake, a crystal casket for the rat, and a golden cage for the parrot [Pragati Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1877]. In the closing identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the wicked prince as Devadatta, the snake as Sāriputta, the rat as Moggallāna, the parrot as Ānanda, and the righteous king as the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1877].

In modern scholarship, the jātaka is frequently analyzed for its thematic treatment of gratitude (*kataññutā*) and the karmic consequences of greed [Anandajoti 2010; Scott 2009]. Pragati Sahni examines the narrative in the context of Buddhist environmental ethics, observing that while the story tames wild creatures with human luxury, its core ethical thrust is the virtue of animal welfare and gratitude [Pragati Sahni 2008].
